knowledge_points.label: Evaluation maps an abstract construct to a concrete metric
knowledge_points.statement: Evaluation asks how 'good' a model is, and its core challenge is turning an abstract construct (good) into a concrete metric; the lecture names four different operationalizations, benchmark scores, benchmark scores per unit cost, human pairwise preference, and revealed usage (what people choose to pay for), each of which answers a different question.

anchors.quote: Evaluation: given a model, how "good" is it?

Evaluation might appear to be a mechanical process ... Define some prompts ... Send prompts to a model and get back responses ... Compute accuracy ... Core challenge ... abstract construct ... concrete metric

Maybe a model is good if it does well on benchmarks ... Maybe a model is good if it does well on benchmarks and is cheap to run ... Maybe a model is good if people prefer its responses ... Maybe a model is good if people simply choose to use (and pay for) it

anchors.ref: Artificial Analysis leaderboards (benchmark index and intelligence-vs-cost, shown at L46 and L49)

anchors.quote: So evaluation might seem like a fairly mechanical process. ... Evaluation sets North Stars and model developers

you start it with an abstract construct of what do I want my model to do? ... Maybe I want my model to be good at conversation or good at reasoning. ... evaluation is really the process of turning that into a concrete metric powered by, presumably, some concrete prompts or environments.
Or maybe a model is good if people simply choose to use it, and therefore, pay for it. ... I don't what good is, but if people are paying for it, it must be good.
So none of those are necessarily the correct answer.

provenance.filtering_note: The three screenshots (artificial-analysis.png, artificial-analysis-cost.png, openrouter.png, L46-L57) carry specific model rankings and scores; none are restated here since they are a snapshot of third-party leaderboards. The professor frames the lecture as a prerequisite to the data lectures ('Before talking about data, need to talk about what behavior we want from a model', L10) and does not define 'construct' or 'metric' beyond the colored arrow at L42; the psychometric sense (construct validity) is implied but not named until validity() at L338. Spoken evidence (1:36-1:57): why evaluation shapes development: 'Evaluation sets North Stars', developers 'look at evaluation as a measure of progress', so choosing an evaluation implicitly shapes what models will be able to do. Correction (partial, 2:01-2:26): the note above says he does not define 'construct' or 'metric' beyond the colored arrow; aloud he illustrates constructs ('good at conversation or good at reasoning') and says the metric is 'powered by, presumably, some concrete prompts or environments'. On the cost screenshot he reads only the qualitative pattern: intelligence and price are correlated 'but it's not exactly aligned' (3:38-3:52). He warns that OpenRouter usage 'is not representative of all model usage' (4:43) and closes with 'none of those are necessarily the correct answer' (5:02).

misconceptions.belief: Evaluation is the mechanical three-step loop: write prompts, collect responses, compute accuracy.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor lists exactly that loop (L35-L37) and then says 'But actually, evaluation is a deep and important topic' (L39): the hard part is the choice of what accuracy on what prompts is supposed to stand for (L42).

misconceptions.belief: A model that leads one leaderboard is the best model.
misconceptions.why_wrong: L44-L55 give four different notions of 'good' (benchmarks, benchmarks per cost, human preference, paid usage) that need not agree, and the final takeaway is 'There is no one true evaluation' (L28).

predict.q: A startup wants to pick a model for a customer-service chatbot and says 'we will take whichever model is highest on the Artificial Analysis intelligence index'. Of the four notions of 'good' the lecture lists, which one does that choice silently assume, and which one is closer to the question they actually have?
predict.answer: It assumes 'does well on benchmarks' (L44). Their question is closer to 'people prefer its responses' or 'cheap to run per benchmark point' (L48, L51), since a support bot is judged by users on open-ended replies and by the company on cost.
predict.why: Each operationalization at L44-L55 answers a different question; the purchase-decision purpose is named explicitly at L374 ('make a purchase decision ... for their use case').
predict.targets_misconception: A model that leads one leaderboard is the best model.

transfer.q: A hospital IT group and a hedge fund each read the same leaderboard that ranks models by OpenRouter token volume. Explain, using the construct-to-metric framing, why the same metric answers a reasonable question for one of them and almost none for the other.
transfer.answer: Token volume operationalizes 'people choose to use and pay for it' (L55), a revealed-preference construct over the general developer population. For a group whose question is 'what do most developers find worth paying for' that is close to the construct; for a group with a specialized, safety-critical use case the construct they care about (clinical accuracy, or domain-specific performance) is not what the metric measures, so the mapping from construct to metric (L42) breaks.
transfer.why: The metric is fixed; whether it is a good proxy depends on the construct the reader cares about, which is exactly the 'abstract construct -> concrete metric' challenge.
transfer.varies: purpose and domain of the reader (two users, same leaderboard); Barnett-Ceci functional context
transfer.invariant: the metric is a proxy for one named construct and is only as good as the match between that construct and the reader's question

check.q: A leaderboard ranks models by OpenRouter token volume. For which reader does that ranking most directly answer the question they actually have?
choices: A buyer asking for the best benchmark score per dollar

A lab asking which model knows the most facts

check.why: Token volume operationalizes 'people choose to use and pay for it' (L55). It matches a question about general developers' revealed preference; clinical accuracy, factual knowledge and cost-normalized benchmark scores are other constructs (L44-L51).

knowledge_points.label: Perplexity (1/p(D))^(1/|D|) and in- vs out-of-distribution evaluation
knowledge_points.statement: Perplexity (1/p(D))^(1/|D|) measures whether a language model p assigns high probability to a dataset D, normalized per token; pre-training minimizes it on the training set, the classic paradigm measured it on the test split of the same dataset (PTB, WikiText-103, One Billion Word), and GPT-2 changed the paradigm by evaluating zero-shot, out of distribution, where transfer helps on small datasets but not on a large one like 1BW.

anchors.quote: a language model is a probability distribution p(x) over sequences of tokens ... Perplexity (1/p(D))^(1/|D|) measures whether p assigns high probability to some dataset D

In pre-training, you minimize perplexity on the training set ... The obvious thing is to measure perplexity on the test set ... Penn Treebank (WSJ) ... WikiText-103 (Wikipedia) ... One Billion Word Benchmark ... Classic paradigm: in-distribution evaluation: train on train split and evaluate on test split of some dataset

Trained on WebText (40GB text, websites linked from Reddit) ... Zero-shot on standard datasets (out-of-distribution evaluation) ... Works better on small datasets (PTB) where transfer is helpful, but not larger datasets (1BW)
Perplexity is still used heavily in language model development (smooth scaling laws)

anchors.ref: Exploring the Limits of Language Modeling (cited at L73 for 'perplexity 51.3 → 30.0' on 1BW)

anchors.quote: a distribution P of x over sequences of tokens. ... there's a very natural way to evaluate a distribution, which is a perplexity, or likelihood or log loss. ... I normalize it and divide so that the numbers are more interpretable.
when we were doing training, we minimized the perplexity on the training set. ... So the obvious thing to do is measure the perplexity on the test set
They evaluated zero-shot on standard data sets that everyone else was evaluating on. ... So this is out-of-distribution evaluation.

So for example, PTB, which is a tiny data set. ... They were getting 35 perplexity compared to the State of The Art, which is 46. ... if you have enough in-distribution data, you don't quite do as well as the SOTA.
Maybe there was some overlap, because I don't know if they did a careful train test decontam.
it is actually still used quite heavily in language model development. ... it's also smoothly varying with scale, which is important for getting scaling laws.

provenance.filtering_note: The GPT-2 perplexity table (images/gpt2-perplexity.png, L78) is the paper's figure; its numbers are shown, not restated, and the 'works better on small datasets ... but not larger datasets (1BW)' reading at L79 is the professor's gloss. The '51.3 → 30.0' at L73 is read off Jozefowicz et al. and quoted with that attribution. The professor writes |D| without saying it counts tokens, and never raises that perplexity is therefore tokenizer-dependent: two models with different vocabularies spread the same total log-probability over different token counts, so per-token perplexities are not comparable across tokenizers unless renormalized per byte or per character using the bytes-per-token compression ratio from lecture 1 (author-inference, not stated in this lecture). He also does not write the log form, exp(-(1/|D|) sum log p(x_i)), which is how it is computed in practice (assignment 1 asks for that). Spoken evidence (8:39-8:48): he reads one cell of the GPT-2 table aloud, PTB perplexity '35 ... compared to the State of The Art, which is 46'; this matches Radford et al. 2019 Table 3 (35.76 vs 46.54), so it is quoted as his reading; no other value from the figure is restated. Spoken evidence (9:05): a caveat the code lacks: the zero-shot gains may partly be overlap, 'I don't know if they did a careful train test decontam.' Spoken evidence (5:49-6:05): the normalization is motivated ('so that the numbers are more interpretable'), but he still never says |D| counts tokens, so the tokenizer remark above stays author inference; he calls perplexity, likelihood and log loss 'all kind of related concepts' (5:36) without writing the log form. Spoken evidence (17:24): perplexity suits scaling laws because it is 'smoothly varying with scale'. Spoken slip (8:53): right after the PTB example he calls the result impressive 'given that this model was not trained on One Billion Word's data set at all'; the example was PTB (L79 contrasts PTB with 1BW), so the dataset is misnamed; not imported.

external_prerequisites.note: |D| at L62 counts tokens; converting a per-token perplexity to a per-byte one divides the exponent by the bytes-per-token ratio from lecture 1. The professor does not make this move; the interactive below does.

misconceptions.belief: A lower perplexity number always means a better language model, whichever two models you compare.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Perplexity is normalized per token (L62), so it depends on the tokenizer and on the dataset; the lecture's own GPT-2 example shows the same model looking good on PTB and worse on 1BW (L79), and nothing in the lecture licenses comparing perplexities across different vocabularies.

misconceptions.belief: Perplexity on a standard test split measures general language ability.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The classic paradigm is in-distribution: train split and test split of the same dataset (L72). GPT-2's move to zero-shot evaluation on those datasets is what made perplexity say something about transfer (L77), and even then it is relative to the dataset's distribution.

predict.q: Two models score the same text. Model A tokenizes it into 1000 tokens and reports perplexity 8. Model B uses a coarser tokenizer that yields 500 tokens, and the total log-probability it assigns to the whole text is exactly the same as A's. Using (1/p(D))^(1/|D|), is B's per-token perplexity lower, equal, or higher than 8, and which model is 'better'?
choices: lower than 8, and B is better
higher than 8, but neither is better
equal to 8, and they tie
predict.answer: higher than 8, but neither is better
predict.why: Evaluating the professor's formula: p(D) is the same for both, so (1/p(D))^(1/500) = 8^(1000/500) = 64 for B. Same total probability spread over half as many tokens doubles the exponent. The models assign identical probability to the text, so the per-token number is an artifact of |D|; the lecture's formula is per token, which is why cross-tokenizer comparison needs a per-byte or per-character renormalization (author-inference, see filtering note).
predict.targets_misconception: A lower perplexity number always means a better language model, whichever two models you compare.

transfer.q: A team pre-trains on a web crawl and reports that their test perplexity on Penn Treebank beats a model that was trained on the Penn Treebank train split, while their perplexity on the One Billion Word test set is worse than the 1BW-trained model. Which of the two evaluation paradigms from the lecture each comparison is, and what mechanism does the professor offer for why the web model wins on one and loses on the other?
transfer.answer: The web-crawl model is being evaluated out of distribution (zero-shot, L77); the dataset-trained baselines are the classic in-distribution paradigm (L72). The professor's mechanism: transfer from a large general corpus helps on a small dataset like PTB, whose own train split is tiny, but not on a large dataset like 1BW, whose in-distribution training data already covers its test distribution (L79).
transfer.why: L72 vs L77 name the two paradigms; L79 gives the small-vs-large dataset explanation read off the GPT-2 results.
transfer.varies: the training distribution of the model under test (web crawl rather than the benchmark's own train split) and the size of the target dataset; functional context of the comparison
transfer.invariant: perplexity still measures p's fit to the specific dataset D; what changes is whether D's distribution was seen during training

check.q: A model pre-trained on a large web crawl is evaluated zero-shot against models trained on each test dataset's own train split. Following the lecture's reading of the GPT-2 results, on which kind of dataset should the web model look best relative to the in-distribution baseline?
choices: One whose own train split is tiny
One whose own train split is huge
Equally on both: perplexity is general
check.answer: One whose own train split is tiny
check.why: Transfer from a large general corpus helps on small datasets (PTB) but not on large ones (1BW), whose own training data already covers the test distribution (L79).
check.varies: the datasets are described by train-split size rather than named
check.invariant: out-of-distribution zero-shot evaluation beats in-distribution training only where in-distribution data is scarce
distractor_from: 'One whose own train split is huge' <- plausible: inverts the small-vs-large explanation
'Equally on both: perplexity is general' <- misconception: 'Perplexity on a standard test split measures general language ability.'
check.targets_misconception: Perplexity on a standard test split measures general language ability.

retrieval.q: Write the perplexity formula as the professor writes it and say what each symbol is.
retrieval.answer: (1/p(D))^(1/|D|): p is the model's probability of the dataset D, and |D| is the number of tokens in D.

retrieval.q: Name the three standard perplexity datasets the lecture lists and their text sources.
retrieval.answer: Penn Treebank (Wall Street Journal), WikiText-103 (Wikipedia), One Billion Word Benchmark (WMT11 machine-translation data: EuroParl, UN, news).

retrieval.q: What does the professor call the 'classic paradigm' of language-model evaluation, and what did GPT-2 do instead?
retrieval.answer: In-distribution evaluation, training on the train split and testing on the test split of one dataset; GPT-2 evaluated zero-shot on those datasets, which is out-of-distribution evaluation.

retrieval.q: Why does the professor say perplexity is still used heavily in model development?
retrieval.answer: Because it gives smooth scaling laws.

presentations.notice: Holding the total log-probability of the text fixed and dragging the token count (tokenizer granularity) changes the per-token perplexity (1/p(D))^(1/|D|), while the per-byte perplexity, which divides the exponent by |D| times bytes-per-token instead, stays put; only the per-byte number is comparable across tokenizers.

knowledge_points.label: 'Perplexity is all you need' vs conditional perplexity on the response
knowledge_points.statement: The faith argument says the best achievable perplexity is the entropy H(t) of the true distribution, reached only when p = t, and such a p would solve every task through p(solution | problem); the counter-argument is that perplexity penalizes prediction on every token, including irrelevant ones like 'founded' in 'Stanford was founded in 1885', so one measures conditional perplexity p(response | prompt)^(1/|response|), which scores only the tokens that matter.

anchors.quote: Perplexity is all you need (more faith than science) ... True distribution is t, model is p ... Best possible perplexity is H(t) obtained iff p = t ... If p = t, then solve all the tasks: p(solution | problem) ... So by pushing down on perplexity, we will eventually "reach AGI"

Perplexity is maybe more than you need ... Example: Stanford was founded in 1885 ... Perplexity penalizes prediction on all tokens, some (e.g., founded) of which might not be relevant ... Solution: measure conditional perplexity p(response | prompt)^(1/|response|)

So there's some true distribution out there-- let's call it t-- and you're training this model p. ... the best perplexity is the entropy of that true distribution, and that is realized when p equals t.
You can condition on a question, generate the answer. ... So by pushing down on perplexity, we'll eventually reach AGI, is the argument.
this is really, I think, a strong driver of many people who have been scaling and scaling language models
perplexity will say, penalize the prediction on all tokens. ... phrased as sentence completion.
And perplexity doesn't care. ... It's going to charge you bits for every bit of a deviation from the true distribution.
you can always measure the conditional perplexity. ... focus on certain tokens that you believe to be relevant and less on others that are sort of incidental.

provenance.filtering_note: The professor writes 'Best possible perplexity is H(t)' (L83); strictly the minimum of cross-entropy is H(t) and the minimum perplexity is exp(H(t)) when H is in nats, so the line conflates the two by a log, a slip the thread notes rather than repeats. The conditional perplexity at L90 is written with a positive exponent 1/|response| on p rather than on 1/p; read with L62 it is the same quantity, the reciprocal convention is inconsistent. He does not say how to choose the prompt/response boundary for a free-text corpus, which is the practical difficulty this idea runs into. Spoken evidence (9:53, 11:08-11:29): he presents the argument as a mindset ('I wouldn't [want] to take this too seriously') that nevertheless drove scaling 'at a time when, maybe, the gains weren't as obvious', before GPT-3. Spoken evidence (11:59-12:41): why '1885' matters and 'founded' does not: the date is a Q&A item 'phrased as sentence completion' and carries world knowledge, while perplexity charges 'bits for every bit of a deviation' on every token. Spoken slip (10:14): 'the best perplexity is the entropy of that true distribution' repeats L83's conflation of H(t) with exp(H(t)); not imported.

prerequisites.note: Conditional perplexity (L90) is the L62 formula restricted to response tokens.

misconceptions.belief: A model with lower perplexity on a corpus is necessarily better at answering the questions contained in that corpus.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Perplexity averages over all tokens (L89); a model can win the average by predicting filler like 'was founded in' better while being no better on the answer token '1885'. That is why the professor proposes conditioning on the prompt and normalizing by the response length (L90).

misconceptions.belief: The 'perplexity is all you need' argument is a theorem about training.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor labels it 'more faith than science' (L81): it says only that the perfect model p = t would solve tasks (L84), not that any finite reduction in perplexity translates into task gains, nor that we can reach p = t.

predict.q: On the sentence 'Stanford was founded in 1885', model X assigns probability 0.5 to each of the four tokens 'Stanford', 'was', 'founded', 'in' and 0.1 to '1885'; model Y assigns 0.25 to each of the first four and 0.4 to '1885'. Which model has lower full-sentence perplexity, and which has lower conditional perplexity on the response '1885' given the prompt?
predict.answer: Full sentence: X, since p_X(D) = 0.5^4 × 0.1 = 0.00625 versus p_Y(D) = 0.25^4 × 0.4 ≈ 0.00156 (evaluating the professor's formula, perplexity X ≈ 2.76 vs Y ≈ 3.64). Conditional on the prompt: Y, since conditional perplexity is 1/0.4 = 2.5 for Y against 1/0.1 = 10 for X.
predict.why: Full perplexity rewards X for the four filler tokens (L89); the conditional version (L90) scores only '1885', the token the question is about, and there Y is four times more confident.
predict.targets_misconception: A model with lower perplexity on a corpus is necessarily better at answering the questions contained in that corpus.

transfer.q: A code-completion team evaluates models by perplexity over whole repositories and finds the ranking disagrees with their users' acceptance rate for completions. Transfer the lecture's 'founded' argument to code: which tokens are the 'founded' tokens here, and what would the analogue of conditional perplexity be?
transfer.answer: Boilerplate, imports, formatting and license headers are the irrelevant tokens that whole-file perplexity rewards predicting (L89); the analogue of conditional perplexity is to condition on the file prefix at the cursor and normalize only over the completion the user actually sees, p(completion | prefix)^(1/|completion|) (L90).
transfer.why: The mechanism is that perplexity penalizes all tokens equally; the fix is to restrict the normalization to the response tokens.
transfer.varies: domain (source code instead of a factual sentence) and what counts as prompt and response
transfer.invariant: perplexity averages over every token, so the metric must be restricted to the tokens the task is about

check.q: Prompt 'The capital of France is' (5 tokens), response 'Paris' (2 tokens: 'Par', 'is'). A model gives each prompt token probability 0.1, and the two response tokens probabilities 0.5 and 0.8 given what precedes them. What is the conditional perplexity (1/p(response | prompt))^(1/|response|)?
check.why: p(response | prompt) = 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4, and (1/0.4)^(1/2) = sqrt(2.5) ≈ 1.58. The prompt-token probabilities do not enter: conditional perplexity scores only the tokens that matter (L90), whereas full-sequence perplexity would be dominated by the 0.1s.
check.varies: a computed number on a new sentence, with irrelevant-token probabilities supplied as a lure
check.invariant: conditional perplexity normalizes only over the response tokens given the prompt
check.targets_misconception: A model with lower perplexity on a corpus is necessarily better at answering the questions contained in that corpus.

retrieval.q: In the 'perplexity is all you need' argument, what is the best possible perplexity and when is it attained?
retrieval.answer: H(t), the entropy of the true distribution t, attained if and only if p = t.

presentations.notice: Drag the prompt boundary k: on the whole sentence X's four cheap filler tokens (1 bit each) pull its average down, so X has the lower perplexity; once only '1885' is scored, Y wins. Perplexity is 2 to the average bits per scored token, and tokens moved into the prompt leave that average entirely.

steps.do: Score the whole sentence 'Stanford was founded in 1885' (5 tokens) under both models.
steps.why: Full perplexity uses the probability of every token, the filler ones included (L89).

steps.do: Apply the perplexity formula (1/p(D))^(1/|D|) from L62 with |D| = 5. X has the lower perplexity.
steps.why: X earns its lead on 'Stanford', 'was', 'founded' and 'in', the tokens the question is not about.

steps.do: Conditional perplexity (L90): the prompt is 'Stanford was founded in', the response is '1885', so |response| = 1.
steps.why: Conditioning on the prompt moves the filler tokens out of the product and out of the normalisation; only the answer is scored.

steps.do: The ranking flips: Y is four times more confident on the answer and now wins, 2.5 against 10.

knowledge_points.label: Log-prob (closed-form) benchmarks vs generation benchmarks
knowledge_points.statement: Some benchmarks are perplexity in disguise: cloze tasks (LAMBADA) and multiple-choice completion (HellaSwag) score a model by the probabilities it assigns to candidate continuations, so a perplexity-style leaderboard must trust that the submitted LM's probabilities are valid (sum to 1), whereas downstream generation tasks only need response = LM(prompt) and compute accuracy on the response.

anchors.quote: Some benchmarks are perplexity in disguise ... Cloze tasks (fill in the blank): LAMBADA ... Multiple choice sentence completion: HellaSwag

Warning (if you're running a perplexity leaderboard) ... People submit LM and you compute log_prob = LM(test_data) ... You need to trust that the probabilities are valid (sum to 1) ... For downstream tasks, response = LM(prompt) and compute accuracy on response
Still need benchmarks that capture real-world situations (for the non-believers)

predict.q: A submission to your perplexity leaderboard returns, for every token, a 'probability' equal to 0.9 regardless of context. knowledge_points.label: MMLU: a multiple-choice exam benchmark that tests knowledge
knowledge_points.statement: Exam benchmarks give control over subject and difficulty and are designed to have an unambiguous, easy-to-grade answer; MMLU is the canonical one, multiple-choice across 57 subjects collected by students from freely available online sources, evaluated on GPT-3 with few-shot prompting, and despite its name it tests knowledge rather than language understanding.

anchors.quote: Exams are a useful way to test language models (as with humans) ... Have control over the subject and difficulty ... Design to have unambiguous correct answer, easy to grade

Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) ... 57 subjects (e.g., math, US history, law, morality), multiple-choice ... collected by graduate and undergraduate students from freely available sources online ... Despite the name, MMLU is really about testing knowledge, not language understanding ... Evaluated on GPT-3 using few-shot prompting

anchors.ref: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding (cited at L113; results figure shown at L118)
HELM MMLU leaderboard for visualizing predictions (cited at L120)

anchors.quote: The nice thing about exams is that you have a very careful control over the subject, over the difficulty. ... You can design them to have unambiguous correct answers, which makes them easy to grade.
We're going to go through 57 subjects ... it's really about testing knowledge and reasoning and less so just pure language understanding.
the way they evaluated it was with GPT-3, using few-shot prompting. ... Some in-context examples of question, answer, question, answer, and then the final question
Some of the small models were barely above chance. ... this benchmark has essentially saturated.

literally you sample and it generates a letter. ... Or more commonly now you generate a chain of thought. ... there is a way of extracting an answer which does matter. ... language model evaluations can be very sensitive to that

The results figure (images/mmlu.png, L118) is the paper's and its accuracies are not restated. The professor says 'few-shot prompting' (L117) without discussing how many shots, whether the answer is scored by log-prob over A/B/C/D or by generated text, or how sensitive scores are to prompt format and option ordering; none of that is in the lecture, so the thread does not assert it. Correction (30:52-31:52, Q&A): the note above says the lecture does not discuss whether the answer is scored by log-prob over A/B/C/D or by generated text, or how sensitive scores are to format. Spoken evidence (20:15-20:33): the few-shot prompt is read aloud ('The following are questions about high school mathematics', question-answer pairs, then the final question). Spoken evidence (19:15-19:36): why MMLU was ahead of its time: around GPT-3 many 'still thought of language models as, well, language models' that generate fluent English. predict.q: A model is fine-tuned heavily on grammar correction and reading-comprehension passages and its MMLU score barely moves, while a model fine-tuned on encyclopedias and textbooks jumps. Which property of MMLU stated in the lecture predicts this?

knowledge_points.label: Saturation drives harder exams: MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HLE
knowledge_points.statement: As models improve and saturate existing benchmarks, exams get harder: MMLU-Pro removes noisy items, widens 4 choices to 10 and grades with chain of thought; GPQA uses PhD-written 'Google-proof' questions where non-experts with web access score far below experts; Humanity's Last Exam filters questions by frontier LLMs through multiple review stages; the multiple-choice format can be made as difficult as one wants, but it still does not capture open-ended real usage.

anchors.quote: MMLU-Pro ... Removed noisy/trivial questions from MMLU ... Expanded 4 choices to 10 choices ... Evaluated using chain of thought (gives model more of a chance) ... Accuracy of models drop by 16% to 33% (not as saturated)

Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A (GPQA) ... Questions written by 61 PhD contractors from Upwork ... PhD experts achieve 65% accuracy ... Non-experts achieve 34% over 30 minutes with access to Google ... GPT-4 achieves 39%

Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) ... 2500 questions: multimodal, many subjects, multiple-choice + short-answer ... Awarded $500K prize pool + co-authorship to question creators ... Filtered by frontier LLMs, multiple stages of review

Trend towards harder questions as models improve and saturate existing benchmarks ... Multiple-choice format can be as difficult as one wants ... Does not capture real usage (open-ended, doesn't necessarily exist correct answer)

anchors.quote: they actually noticed that there was some noisy and trivial problems, so let's get rid of them. ... Four choices might be a little bit too easy, so let's expand that to 10. ... it's clear that some of these questions could benefit from a few reasoning steps.
if you can solve a problem by looking at Google. ... So if you can just solve it then that's probably too easy.
You actually have to go through quite a bit of human labor to get really hard questions. ... So this was 61 PhD contractors from Upwork.
there's a subset of these questions called the DIAMOND set
And PhD experts were only able to get 65%. ... So this is I think mostly four-way multiple choice. ... they were getting a bit over chance, but not much.
So these benchmarks have a shelf life of not too high I guess. ... they're still useful for developing smaller models or fitting scaling laws and so on.
They had some money to incentivize people who were into money to create questions. ... they went through multiple stages of reviews filtered by frontier models.
So every data set paper looks like this. ... Previous benchmarks, look the models are doing so well. ... My data set, look all the models are doing really poorly.
with multiple choice, I mean, you can make it as difficult as you want. ... multiple choice restricts the set of questions you can ask.
The main problem with exam-based questions is that this does not capture real-world usage. ... No one asks HLE questions to a language model except for when you're evaluating on HLE.

HLE's 'filtered by frontier LLMs' (L144) is adversarial filtering: keep questions current models get wrong, which the professor states but does not name. He also does not raise that adversarially filtered benchmarks measure a moving target relative to the filtering models. He still does not explain why 10 options lower scores. knowledge_points.label: Chatbot Arena: pairwise human preference fit by an Elo model
knowledge_points.statement: Chatbot Arena collects a prompt from an anonymous user, shows responses from two anonymized models, records which the user prefers, and turns the pairwise outcomes into a ranking by fitting p(A wins against B) = 1 / (1 + 10^((ELO_B - ELO_A)/400)) to maximize the probability of the observed comparisons.

anchors.quote: Most people don't ask multiple-choice exam questions to their AI assistant ... Challenge: how to evaluate an open-ended response?
Chatbot Arena ... Random person from the Internet types in prompt ... They get response from two random (anonymized) models ... They rate which one is better
Compute ELO rankings based on pairwise comparisons ... Define model: p(A wins against B) = 1 / (1 + 10^((ELO_B - ELO_A)/400)) ... Fit this model to maximize probability of pairwise comparisons

anchors.ref: Chatbot Arena paper (cited at L165; side-by-side screenshot shown at L170)
Arena AI leaderboard (cited at L174; screenshot shown at L175)

anchors.quote: any random person from the internet can go in and chat. ... you actually get two responses from two different models which are anonymized, and then they rate which one is better.
A is better, both are good, both are bad, B is better?
So it's a smooth mapping. ... you fit this model with the parameters, which are the ELO ratings to maximize the probability of the pairwise comparisons

provenance.filtering_note: The professor writes the Elo logistic with base 10 and scale 400 (L172) and says 'fit to maximize probability' (L173) without noting that this is the Bradley-Terry model of lecture 15 in a different parametrization (10^(x/400) = exp(x·ln10/400), so an Elo gap of 400 is a logit gap of ln 10 ≈ 2.3). He does not mention ties, the online update form of Elo versus a batch maximum-likelihood fit, or confidence intervals, all of which the cited paper discusses. Evaluating his formula: a 400-point gap gives 10/11 ≈ 0.909, a 200-point gap about 0.76, a 100-point gap about 0.64, and a common shift of both ratings leaves p unchanged. No score from the leaderboard screenshot (L175) is restated. Correction (33:38-33:49): the note above says the professor does not mention ties; reading the Arena interface he lists four buttons, 'A is better, both are good, both are bad, B is better', so tied outcomes are collected. He does not say how ties enter the fit, and L172 has no tie term. Spoken evidence (34:11-34:48): the rating model is 'a smooth mapping' from rating difference to win probability, fit by maximum likelihood. Spoken evidence (37:57): sparse battles suffice 'as long as the graph is connected'; that condition became the spoken KP elo-needs-connected-comparisons. No leaderboard score is restated (35:06 names only the leading model family).

prerequisites.note: Arena is introduced as the answer to 'does not capture real usage' (L152, L156-L157).

external_prerequisites.note: Same model, different parametrization: sigmoid(r_A - r_B) with r = ELO · ln10/400. Lecture 15 derives it for reward modelling; lecture 12 uses it to rank models.
The data-collection protocol at L166-L169 is pairwise feedback from an uncontrolled crowd.

misconceptions.belief: An Arena rating is an absolute score, so a rating of 1300 means the same quality in any arena.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The model at L172 depends only on the difference ELO_B - ELO_A, so adding a constant to every model's rating leaves every predicted win probability unchanged; ratings are identified only relative to the pool of models being compared.

misconceptions.belief: Arena shows every model the same set of prompts so the comparison is fair.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Each user's prompt is answered by two random models (L168), and the professor lists as a feature that one does not need to feed the same prompts to all models (L181); the pairwise model is what makes sparse, non-aligned comparisons combinable.

predict.q: Two models sit 400 Elo points apart on the Arena leaderboard. A new, much stronger model then enters and every existing rating, including these two, is shifted down by 100 points. Using the professor's formula, what fraction of head-to-head votes between the original two should the higher-rated one now win, as a decimal?
predict.answer: About 0.91 (10/11); unchanged after a common shift.
predict.why: Evaluating the professor's formula at L172: 1/(1 + 10^(-400/400)) = 1/(1 + 0.1) = 10/11. Only the difference ELO_B - ELO_A enters, so shifting both by the same amount changes nothing.
predict.targets_misconception: An Arena rating is an absolute score, so a rating of 1300 means the same quality in any arena.

transfer.q: A university runs a 'teaching assistant arena' where students submit a question, get two anonymized TA answers, and vote. One TA only ever appears paired against the weakest TA, because of scheduling. Explain, using the fitted-model view at L172-L173, why that TA's rating is still meaningful in principle, and what about the data would make it unreliable.
transfer.answer: The rating is fit by maximizing the likelihood of all pairwise outcomes under one shared model (L173), so a TA compared only to the weakest TA is placed relative to that TA, who is in turn placed relative to everyone else; comparisons chain through the pool, which is why Arena need not show the same prompts to all models (L181). It becomes unreliable because the rating is pinned down only through one neighbour: few comparisons and a single path give a wide uncertainty, and any bias in that one pairing (prompt mix, time of day) propagates directly.
transfer.why: Maximum-likelihood fitting of a pairwise model transfers information along comparison chains; sparse, non-random pairing is the weak point.
transfer.varies: domain (teaching assistants instead of chatbots) and a structurally sparse comparison graph
transfer.invariant: ratings are fit jointly from pairwise outcomes and are identified only relative to the pool

check.q: Under the professor's formula p(A beats B) = 1 / (1 + 10^((ELO_B − ELO_A)/400)), model A is rated 100 points above B, and B 200 points above C. A and C have never been paired. What fraction of A-vs-C votes should A win? Give a decimal.
check.why: One shared fitted model places every rating on one scale, so A is 300 above C: 1/(1 + 10^(−0.75)) = 1/1.178 ≈ 0.85. Comparisons chain through the pool, which is why Arena need not pair every model (L173, L181).
check.varies: the chain is computed numerically for a pair that never met
check.invariant: ratings come from one maximum-likelihood fit, so information passes along chains of comparisons
check.targets_misconception: Arena shows every model the same set of prompts so the comparison is fair.

retrieval.answer: A random internet user types a prompt; receives responses from two random anonymized models; rates which is better.

retrieval.q: Write the win-probability model the professor uses for Elo.
retrieval.answer: p(A wins against B) = 1 / (1 + 10^((ELO_B - ELO_A)/400)).

retrieval.q: How are the Elo ratings determined from the data?
retrieval.answer: By fitting the model to maximize the probability of the observed pairwise comparisons.

retrieval.q: Why does the professor say Chatbot Arena is needed after the exam benchmarks?

prompts.self_explain: Why does a pairwise comparison between two responses to the same prompt give cleaner signal than asking a rater to score one response on a 1-10 scale?

presentations.notice: Only rating differences are fitted: 'shift every rating' slides every node together and leaves every win probability and the log-likelihood unchanged, and two linked gaps add, so A's win probability over C follows from A–B and B–C battles alone.

The predicted win probability depends only on the rating difference: sliding both ratings together leaves p fixed, while widening the gap pushes p toward 1 along a logistic curve (an Elo gap of 400 corresponds to 10/11; the fixture's sigmoid of a reward difference is the same curve with the gap rescaled by ln10/400).

knowledge_points.label: What Arena buys and what it conflates
knowledge_points.statement: Arena-style evaluation has real-world prompts because the service is free and useful, does not require the same prompts for every model, and is dynamic as new prompts and models arrive, but the raters are an unknown, possibly biased or spamming population, the binary preference conflates style with correctness, and raters may be unable to assess correctness and prone to rewarding sycophancy.

anchors.quote: Real-world prompts (free for users, incentives to actually use it) ... But who are these people? biases? spammers? ... Binary preference but conflates style and correctness ... How does the human even assess correctness?  Prone to sycophancy? ... Feature: don't need to feed same prompts to all models (important because human is rating) ... Dynamic: incorporates new prompts and models over time

Pairwise comparisons between similar responses provide higher signal ... Beware of biases (both from humans and LLM judges) ... Checklist/rubric improves reliability (regardless of human or LLM judge)
Chatbot Arena prompts are from real people, but distribution is uncontrolled
One is that you have real-world prompts. ... the incentive for someone to come to the site is that they get free access to a language model.
But one thing you should keep in mind is, who are these people? ... Maybe spammers. ... who maybe even submitted a model and they want their model to look good.
does conflate style and correctness. ... So ELO ratings for chess makes a lot of sense, because the only thing that matters is, did you win?
they're presumably asking the question because they don't know the answer. ... And then there's also the problem of sycophancy
you don't need to feed the same prompts to all the models, and this is the beauty of ELO. ... you can't expect a human to rate all the models or even more than two models.
as new prompts and new models come in, there's a natural story for making this updating over time.

Pairwise comparisons between a reference and a model response is generally a good idea ... especially for very similar responses, you can give directional information. ... That tends to be a lot less high signal.
One should always be aware of biases both in terms of humans or LLM judges. ... you evaluate over multiple judges

it's important to define rubrics or checklists to improve the reliability ... if you just ask a human to rate something without giving some of rubric, you're probably going to get very nonsensical results.

provenance.filtering_note: The six bullets at L177-L182 are raised as questions ('who are these people?', 'Prone to sycophancy?') rather than findings; the lecture does not cite evidence on rater demographics, vote manipulation, or style effects in Arena specifically. The length/style bias is documented in the lecture only for the LLM judge in AlpacaEval (L187); for human raters it is asserted as a concern. prerequisites.note: Properties (L176) are listed immediately after the mechanism.

external_prerequisites.note: 'Conflates style and correctness' (L179) is the evaluation-side face of the style and length effects lecture 15 documents for human and GPT judges.

misconceptions.belief: Because Arena prompts come from real users, the Arena ranking measures real-world usefulness.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The prompts are real but their distribution is uncontrolled (L317) and the raters are an unknown population (L178); a binary preference also folds style into the verdict (L179), so the ranking measures what these raters prefer on what they happen to ask.

misconceptions.belief: Human raters are the gold standard for correctness.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor asks how the human even assesses correctness and whether the rating is prone to sycophancy (L180): a rater without domain knowledge can prefer the confident, agreeable answer over the right one.

predict.q: A model developer fine-tunes a model to add confident, flattering openers ('Great question! Here is the definitive answer...') and more formatting, without changing the factual content. Predict the direction its Arena rating moves (start your answer with up, down or same), then name the Arena property from L176-L182 that predicts it.
predict.answer: up: the binary preference conflates style and correctness (L179) and raters who cannot assess correctness may reward sycophancy (L180)
predict.why: Nothing about correctness changed, so any movement comes through the style channel the lecture flags.
predict.targets_misconception: Human raters are the gold standard for correctness.

transfer.q: A hospital wants to rank two diagnostic assistants by letting clinicians vote pairwise in a private arena. Name the two Arena weaknesses from the lecture this setup fixes and the one it does not, and say what the lecture recommends to improve the remaining one.
transfer.answer: It fixes 'who are these people?' (known, qualified raters rather than anonymous internet users, L178) and 'how does the human assess correctness?' (clinicians can, L180). It does not fix the conflation of style and correctness in a binary preference (L179). The lecture's recommendation is a checklist or rubric, which 'improves reliability (regardless of human or LLM judge)' (L205).
transfer.why: Rater identity and competence are properties of the crowd; style conflation is a property of the binary-preference instrument.
transfer.varies: the rater population (expert, known) and the deployment domain
transfer.invariant: a binary pairwise preference mixes style and correctness unless the instrument itself is changed

check.q: An arena keeps its anonymous raters but replaces the single binary vote with separate ratings for correctness and for style. Which Arena weakness from the lecture does this change target?
choices: Prompts differ across models
Unknown rater population
Raters spamming or biased
Style conflated with correctness
check.why: The binary preference conflates style and correctness (L179); splitting the instrument addresses that. Rater identity and spam are crowd properties the change leaves alone (L178), and differing prompts are a feature, not a weakness (L181).
check.varies: the fix is to the instrument (the vote format), not to the crowd
check.invariant: rater identity and competence are crowd properties; style conflation is a property of the binary-preference instrument
distractor_from: 'Unknown rater population' <- plausible: a real weakness, but of the crowd, which is unchanged
'Raters spamming or biased' <- plausible: a crowd weakness the vote format does not touch
'Prompts differ across models' <- misconception: 'Arena shows every model the same set of prompts so the comparison is fair' (inverted: treats differing prompts as the flaw)

retrieval.answer: The service is free for users, so there is an incentive to actually use it.

retrieval.q: What does the professor say a binary preference conflates?
retrieval.answer: Style and correctness.

retrieval.answer: You do not need to feed the same prompts to all models.

retrieval.answer: A checklist or rubric.

knowledge_points.label: Elo needs a connected comparison graph, not every pair
knowledge_points.statement: Elo (Bradley-Terry) ratings do not need every pair of models compared or every model shown the same prompts: a sparse sample of pairwise battles suffices as long as the comparison graph (models as nodes, battles as edges) is connected, because only rating differences enter p(A wins against B); models in components that are never linked, directly or through a chain of other models, have no defined rating offset, so their ratings cannot be compared.

anchors.quote: you don't need to feed the same prompts to all the models, and this is the beauty of ELO. ... In chess, you don't have to play. ... It can just be some sparse sample of that. ... And you can still derive rankings as long as the graph is connected.
you can't expect a human to rate all the models or even more than two models.

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only (37:42-38:02). The code says only 'Feature: don't need to feed same prompts to all models (important because human is rating)' (L181); the condition is spoken: 'you can still derive rankings as long as the graph is connected', contrasted with chess where not 'everyone plays everyone else'. Why connectivity is the condition is the author's derivation from L172: p depends only on ELO_B - ELO_A, so adding a constant to every rating in one component leaves every observed probability unchanged, and any battle linking two components (directly or via intermediate models) pins their offset. Connectivity is necessary, not sufficient, for a finite maximum-likelihood fit: with very few links and one-sided outcomes the fitted gap can diverge (the classical condition is strong connectivity of the win graph, Ford 1957); the prompts stay at the professor's level. The checkpoint-chain transfer is the author's changed case. Placed after arena-properties-biases, inside whose stretch it is said.

prerequisites.note: The rating model whose identifiability is at stake.

misconceptions.belief: To rank N models with Elo, every pair of models (or at least every model on the same prompts) must be compared directly.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A sparse sample is enough 'as long as the graph is connected' (37:57): only rating differences matter, and they chain through intermediate models.

misconceptions.belief: Elo ratings fitted from separate pools of battles are on one common scale and can be compared directly.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Within a pool nothing fixes the overall level: adding a constant to every rating in it leaves every p(A wins against B) at L172 unchanged, so the offset between two never-linked pools is arbitrary.

predict.q: Two groups of models were rated from separate pools of battles that never share a battle. After fitting, group 1's ratings sit near 1300 and group 2's near 1100. What does this say about group 1 versus group 2?
choices: Group 1 is better: a 200-point gap is about a 0.76 win rate
Nothing: each group's level is arbitrary without linking battles
Group 1 is better, but only if both pools used the same prompts
They are equal: ratings from separate pools average out
predict.answer: Nothing: each group's level is arbitrary without linking battles
predict.why: p(A wins against B) depends only on the rating difference (L172), so shifting all of group 2 up by 200 fits its own battles exactly as well. With no battle connecting the groups, the 200-point gap is not identified ('as long as the graph is connected', 37:57).
predict.targets_misconception: Elo ratings fitted from separate pools of battles are on one common scale and can be compared directly.
predict.distractor_from: 'Group 1 is better: 200-point gap' <- misconception: separate pools share a scale (the 0.76 is the right formula applied to an undefined gap); 'only if same prompts' <- confuses prompt overlap with comparison links; 'equal' <- assumes each pool centres at the same mean, which is a convention, not a measurement

transfer.q: You run human pairwise evaluation of 6 training checkpoints. To save rater time, raters only ever compare consecutive checkpoints (1 vs 2, 2 vs 3, ..., 5 vs 6). Can checkpoint 1 and checkpoint 6 be placed on one Elo scale? What changes if all the 3-vs-4 comparisons are lost?
transfer.answer: Yes: the chain 1-2-3-4-5-6 is a connected graph, so 1 and 6 are linked through intermediate checkpoints even though they never meet. Without the 3-vs-4 comparisons the graph splits into {1,2,3} and {4,5,6}, and ratings across the split are no longer comparable.
transfer.why: Elo only needs a connected comparison graph (37:57); a missing bridge edge disconnects it and leaves the offset between the two halves free.
transfer.varies: the setting moves from a public arena to an internal checkpoint study with a chain-shaped comparison graph
transfer.invariant: ratings are comparable exactly within connected components of the comparison graph

check.q: An arena has models A, B, C, which have only ever battled each other, and models D, E, F, which have only ever battled each other. Which additional data makes A's and D's ratings comparable?
choices: Battles between any model of the first group and any of the second
Direct A-versus-D battles only; other cross pairs do not help
More battles within each group, to make each group more precise
None: Elo ratings already sit on one absolute scale
check.answer: Battles between any model of the first group and any of the second
check.why: Any cross-group battle connects the comparison graph, and differences chain through B, C, E, F, so A and D become comparable without ever meeting. More within-group battles leave the graph disconnected.
check.varies: asks which data would fix the problem instead of interpreting a gap
check.invariant: comparability requires a connected comparison graph, not direct comparisons
distractor_from: 'Direct A-versus-D battles only' <- misconception: every pair must be compared directly
'More battles within each group' <- plausible: confuses precision with identifiability
'None: one absolute scale' <- misconception: separate pools share a scale
check.targets_misconception: To rank N models with Elo, every pair of models (or at least every model on the same prompts) must be compared directly.

retrieval.q: What condition on the battles lets Elo derive rankings without everyone playing everyone?
retrieval.answer: The comparison graph must be connected.

retrieval.q: Why must Arena work without feeding every model the same prompts?
retrieval.answer: Humans do the rating, and a human cannot rate all the models, or even more than two, on one prompt.

prompts.self_explain: Why does the win probability depending only on ELO_B - ELO_A mean that two never-linked groups have no comparable ratings?

presentations.notice: With no battle between the two pools, the offset slider moves the orange component and its win probability against A while the log-likelihood stays put, so the gap is not identified; switching on any one cross battle (C–D or B–E) joins the graph, turns every node blue and fixes the gap.
listen for: 'you can still derive rankings as long as the graph is connected'

knowledge_points.label: LLM-as-judge: AlpacaEval's length gaming, debiasing, and validation against humans
knowledge_points.statement: AlpacaEval scores a model by its win rate against a GPT-4-preview baseline as judged by GPT-4 preview on a fixed set of instructions; the judge favored longer responses, which was gamed on the leaderboard, so AlpacaEval 2.0 used regression to debias length, and the metric itself is validated by its high correlation with Chatbot Arena's human preferences; WildBench adds a checklist to the LLM judge, acting like chain of thought for judging.

anchors.quote: AlpacaEval (2023) ... 805 instructions from various sources ... Metric: win rate against baseline model (GPT-4 preview) as judged by GPT-4 preview (potential bias?) ... Problem: LLM judges favor longer responses, resulted in leaderboard gaming ... Alpaca Eval 2.0 used regression to debias the metric ... How do we evaluate the metric? ... Correlation with Chatbot Arena (humans) is high

WildBench ... Sourced 1024 examples from 1M human-chatbot conversations ... Uses GPT-4 turbo as a judge with a checklist (like CoT for judging) + GPT-4 as a judge ... Well-correlated with Chatbot Arena (seems to be the de facto sanity check)

anchors.ref: AlpacaEval leaderboard (cited at L184; screenshot shown at L192)
WildBench paper (cited at L194; figure shown at L198)

anchors.quote: the metric here is the win rate against a baseline model. ... So immediately, this raises a question of potential bias.
this is basically an instantiation of LLM as a judge ... you can mitigate this bias by having multiple judges and ensembling
LLM judges favor long responses. ... they got really high LLM AlpacaEval performance just because the responses were longer. ... use a very simple regression method to de-bias the metric.
how do you evaluate a metric? ... you can look at correlation with other metrics
So AlpacaEval correlation with Chatbot Arena is 0.98 which is quite high.
The main innovation here is the use of a checklist, which is generated and specific to a particular prompt or task. ... This is in some sense a very ill-defined task.

provenance.filtering_note: '805 instructions' and '1024 examples from 1M conversations' are read off the papers and quoted with that attribution; the correlation values in the alpaca_eval figure (L191) and the WildBench figure (L198) are shown, not restated. The professor flags 'potential bias?' (L186) about a GPT-4 judge grading a GPT-4 baseline (self-preference) but does not pursue it, and does not name other documented judge biases (position bias, verbosity beyond length, self-enhancement). 'Regression to debias' (L188) is not unpacked: the cited paper fits a logistic regression with a length-difference term and reports the win rate with that term zeroed out. The claim that correlation with Arena validates a metric (L190, L197) is itself a construct-to-metric move: it takes human preference as the reference construct. Spoken evidence (39:16): a mitigation for the self-preference bias he flags: 'having multiple judges and ensembling'; he still names no other judge biases. Spoken evidence (40:36): he reads one value of the alpaca_eval figure aloud, AlpacaEval's correlation with Chatbot Arena 'is 0.98', quoted as his reading. Spoken evidence (40:20-41:22, 42:53): what that correlation does and does not license (a stand-in for the reference only, over the measured models only, circular if the reference is not ground truth); that became the spoken KP judge-correlation-validity-range. Spoken evidence (42:26-42:53): why WildBench's checklist helps: asking a judge whether a response is good 'is in some sense a very ill-defined task', and a prompt-specific checklist 'greatly scopes' it. He adds that the AlpacaEval leaderboard 'hasn't been maintained in over a year' (41:22).

prerequisites.note: Arena's human preferences are the reference against which AlpacaEval and WildBench are validated (L190, L197).

external_prerequisites.note: L187 'LLM judges favor longer responses' is the same length effect lecture 15 documents for GPT-based and human judges; lecture 12 shows its consequence on a leaderboard and one fix.

misconceptions.belief: An LLM judge removes human bias from evaluation.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The lecture's first LLM-judge example is a bias story: the judge favored longer responses and the leaderboard was gamed until the metric was regression-debiased (L187-L188). The summary says to beware biases 'from humans and LLM judges' (L204).

misconceptions.belief: A judge-based metric is validated by checking that it agrees with itself across runs.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor's answer to 'How do we evaluate the metric?' (L189) is external: correlation with Chatbot Arena's human votes (L190), which he calls the de facto sanity check (L197). Consistency is not validity.

predict.q: Under the original AlpacaEval metric, a team ships a system prompt that appends two paragraphs of restated context to every answer. Predict the direction of its win rate under the original metric and under the length-controlled AlpacaEval 2.0, and say what each prediction rests on.
predict.answer: Original: win rate goes up, because the GPT-4 judge favors longer responses (L187). Length-controlled 2.0: little or no change, because the regression removes the part of the win rate explained by length difference (L188). The first rests on judge bias; the second on the debiasing having modelled exactly that bias.
predict.why: The lecture presents 2.0 as the fix for precisely this leaderboard gaming.
predict.targets_misconception: An LLM judge removes human bias from evaluation.

transfer.q: A newsroom builds an LLM judge to rate headline quality and reports that it agrees with itself 97% of the time on re-runs. Using the lecture's treatment of AlpacaEval and WildBench, name what is still missing before the judge's score can be trusted, and one design change the lecture associates with more reliable judging.
transfer.answer: Missing: validation against an external reference of the construct, which for the lecture is correlation with human preferences (Chatbot Arena, L190, L197); self-agreement says nothing about whether the judge tracks what humans mean by quality, and it could be systematically biased (e.g. toward longer headlines, L187). Design change: give the judge a checklist or rubric, which WildBench does ('like CoT for judging', L196) and the summary endorses for any judge (L205).
transfer.why: Validity is agreement with the construct's reference measurement, not reproducibility; checklists make the judgment more reliable.
transfer.varies: domain (headlines instead of chatbot responses) and the evidence offered (self-consistency instead of human correlation)
transfer.invariant: a judge-based metric must be checked against an external reference and is helped by a rubric

check.q: A team builds an LLM judge for summary quality and wants to validate it before relying on it. Which evidence does the lecture treat as validation of a judge-based metric?
choices: High correlation with human preference ratings
High agreement with itself across re-runs
Being a stronger model than those it judges
Low variance of its scores across prompts
check.answer: High correlation with human preference ratings
check.why: AlpacaEval is validated by its high correlation with Chatbot Arena's human preferences (L190); self-agreement and judge strength say nothing about whether it tracks the construct, and the GPT-4 judge was itself biased toward length (L187).
check.varies: a new task (summaries) and a choice among kinds of evidence
check.invariant: validity is agreement with an external reference of the construct, not reproducibility
distractor_from: 'High agreement with itself across re-runs' <- misconception: 'A judge-based metric is validated by checking that it agrees with itself across runs.'
'Being a stronger model than those it judges' <- misconception: 'An LLM judge removes human bias from evaluation.'
'Low variance of its scores across prompts' <- plausible: mistakes stability for validity
check.targets_misconception: A judge-based metric is validated by checking that it agrees with itself across runs.

retrieval.q: What is AlpacaEval's metric, including who the baseline is and who judges?
retrieval.answer: Win rate against a GPT-4-preview baseline, as judged by GPT-4 preview.

retrieval.q: What bias of LLM judges does the professor say led to leaderboard gaming, and how did AlpacaEval 2.0 respond?
retrieval.answer: Favoring longer responses; 2.0 used regression to debias the metric.

retrieval.q: How does the professor answer 'How do we evaluate the metric?'
retrieval.answer: By its correlation with Chatbot Arena (human preferences), which is high.

retrieval.q: What does WildBench add to the LLM judge, and what does the professor compare it to?
retrieval.answer: A checklist, which he likens to chain of thought for judging.

prompts.self_explain: Why would a judge model prefer longer responses even when the extra text adds nothing, and why does that bias get amplified once the judge drives a leaderboard?

presentations.notice: Padding B moves its raw win rate up the S-curve and can lift it past A, while B's length-controlled win rate (dashed) does not move: the regression reads the judge at zero length difference. With φ = 0 the two lines coincide and padding buys nothing.

knowledge_points.label: A metric's correlation with a reference holds only for the models it was measured on
knowledge_points.statement: A high correlation between a new metric and a reference (AlpacaEval against Chatbot Arena) licenses using the metric as a stand-in for that reference only over the population of models on which the correlation was measured: it may not hold for models stronger than the judge, and a higher correlation is better only if mimicking the reference is the goal, which is circular when the reference itself is not ground truth.

anchors.quote: But if I'm coming up with a metric, how do this metric is any good? ... you can look at correlation with other metrics with the idea that higher isn't necessarily better in all cases unless you are trying to mimic this other metric.

you can use AlpacaEval to evaluate instead. ... Now, this correlation, of course, is with respect to a certain set of models. ... this might not hold for models that let's say are stronger than GPT-4 preview.
which admittedly is a little bit circular because then you can ask why, well, is Chatbot Arena really the ground truth?

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only (40:14-41:22, 42:53-43:06). The code asks 'How do we evaluate the metric?' and answers 'Correlation with Chatbot Arena (humans) is high' (L189-L190), calling Arena correlation 'the de facto sanity check' (L197); the limits are spoken: the correlation 'is with respect to a certain set of models' and 'might not hold for models that let's say are stronger than GPT-4 preview' (the judge); 'higher isn't necessarily better in all cases unless you are trying to mimic this other metric'; and correlating WildBench with Arena is 'a little bit circular'. The 0.98 is the professor's reading of the alpaca_eval figure (40:36). Why stronger-than-judge models are the risky case (a judge may not separate responses better than its own) is the author's gloss on his example; the reading-level transfer is the author's changed case. Placed after llm-judge-length-bias, inside whose stretch it is said.

prerequisites.note: The metric and the validation-by-correlation being qualified.

misconceptions.belief: A metric that correlates 0.98 with human preference can stand in for human evaluation on any model.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The correlation was measured on a particular set of models; 'this might not hold for models that let's say are stronger than GPT-4 preview' (41:13).

misconceptions.belief: The higher a new metric's correlation with an existing benchmark, the better the new metric.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Only if the goal is to mimic that benchmark (40:20). If the reference is not ground truth, agreeing with it copies its biases, which is why validating against Arena is 'a little bit circular' (42:53).

predict.q: AlpacaEval (judged by GPT-4 preview) correlates 0.98 with Chatbot Arena over the models on its 2023 leaderboard. A lab now uses it to choose between two new models, both clearly stronger than GPT-4 preview. How much does the 0.98 tell them?
choices: Little: it was measured on models weaker than the judge
A lot: 0.98 means it matches Arena on any model
A lot, as long as the length bias has been removed
Little: correlations above 0.9 are usually by chance
predict.answer: Little: it was measured on models weaker than the judge
predict.why: 'this correlation, of course, is with respect to a certain set of models. And so this might not hold for models that let's say are stronger than GPT-4 preview' (41:07-41:22).
predict.targets_misconception: A metric that correlates 0.98 with human preference can stand in for human evaluation on any model.
predict.distractor_from: 'A lot: matches Arena on any model' <- misconception: the correlation transfers to any model; 'A lot, once length is debiased' <- fixes a different flaw (length bias) and keeps the extrapolation; 'Little: chance' <- right verdict for a wrong reason (0.98 over many models is not chance)

transfer.q: A reading-level formula was validated on school textbooks, where it correlates 0.9 with teachers' difficulty ratings. A publisher now wants to use it to grade the difficulty of legal contracts. What should they check before trusting it, and why?
transfer.answer: Re-validate it on contracts, against expert ratings of contracts: the 0.9 holds only over the population it was measured on (textbooks), and contracts lie outside that population, so the formula may rank them badly.
transfer.why: A correlation licenses substitution only over the population and reference it was measured against (41:07).
transfer.varies: the domain moves from LLM judges to a readability formula, and the out-of-range population is a new genre instead of stronger models
transfer.invariant: validation by correlation does not extrapolate beyond the measured population

check.q: Metric M is meant to replace human ratings for ranking chatbots. Which validation result best supports using M to rank a new generation of models?
choices: Correlation with human ratings measured on models like the new ones
A 0.99 correlation with an older metric on last year's models
A 0.98 correlation with humans on last year's weaker models
High agreement of M with itself across repeated runs
check.answer: Correlation with human ratings measured on models like the new ones
check.why: Only a correlation with the reference you want to replace, measured on the population you will use it on, supports the substitution (40:20-41:22). Last year's weaker models are outside that population, another metric is not the human reference, and self-agreement is reliability, not validity.
check.varies: chooses the validation evidence instead of interpreting a given correlation
check.invariant: a correlation supports substitution only over the population and the reference it was measured against
distractor_from: '0.99 with an older metric' <- misconception: higher correlation with any benchmark means a better metric
'0.98 with humans on last year's weaker models' <- misconception: the correlation holds for any model
'agreement with itself' <- lecture misconception (llm-judge-length-bias): a judge metric is validated by self-agreement
check.targets_misconception: A metric that correlates 0.98 with human preference can stand in for human evaluation on any model.

knowledge_points.label: Agentic benchmarks evaluate the scaffold together with the model
knowledge_points.statement: Agentic benchmarks evaluate what a language model does rather than what it says, on tasks that require tool use and iteration over time (SWE-bench: codebase plus issue to PR graded by unit tests; Terminal-Bench; Cybench CTFs with first-solve time as difficulty; MLE-bench Kaggle competitions); because an agent is a language model plus a scaffold (planning, delegation to sub-agents, persistent memory, process instructions), the score is a property of the scaffold-model pair, not of the model alone.

anchors.quote: Previously: evaluate what LMs say (chat) ... Now: evaluate what LMs do (agents) ... Agent = language model + agent scaffold (logic for deciding how to use the LM) ... Consider tasks that require tool use (e.g., running code) and iterating over a period of time
SWEBench ... 2294 tasks across 12 Python repositories ... Given codebase + issue description, submit a PR ... Evaluation metric: unit tests
CyBench ... 40 Capture the Flag (CTF) tasks ... Use first-solve time as a measure of difficulty

Agent scaffolds ... Explicit planning: keep a todo list that gets checked off ... Hierarchical delegation: agents calling other sub-agents (clean context) ... Persistent memory: read/write files ... Extreme context engineering ... Agents dramatically enhance the capability surface of language models ... Agent scaffolds are very important ... Evaluating agents = evaluating agent scaffold + language model

anchors.ref: SWE-bench paper (cited at L216; figure shown at L220)
Terminal-Bench paper and website (cited at L223; figures shown at L224-L228)
Cybench paper (cited at L231; figures shown at L232-L236)
MLE-bench paper (cited at L239; figures shown at L241-L242)
Agents 2.0 / deep agents post (cited at L244; overview figure shown at L245)

anchors.quote: evaluate what language models say, and that's chat. ... now, we're going to evaluate what LLMs do, which is agents.
So Agent is basically a language model plus some scaffold, which is a logic for deciding how the language model is going to be called and what tools it can has access to
you're given a code base and a description of a GitHub issue, submit a PR. ... And the way you evaluate a PR is whether it passes the unit test.
And these tasks were crowdsourced from 93 people from across the world. ... 89 of these tasks are constitute Terminal-Bench 2.0.
the agent is also important here because you can have two agents but the same model and they have different accuracies.
the goal is to essentially hack into this server to extract some flag, which is a unique string that proves that you've hacked into the server.
This is a very simplistic version where basically you have one continuous memory. ... this history obviously grows quite a bit.
there's quite a bit of variation in terms of the different agent scaffolds. ... they matter a lot.
explicit planning is helpful. ... Hierarchical delegation, agents should call other sub-agents with some clean context.
And these things are generally optimized for the particular language model. ... when we talk about evaluating agents, it's evaluating both the language model and the agent scaffold.

Cybench's 'first-solve time' (L234) is human first-solve time in the CTF competition, used as a difficulty proxy; he does not elaborate. The dataset-quality problems of agentic benchmarks (insufficient tests, trivial agents passing) are deferred to validity() at L367. Spoken evidence (46:18-46:29): how SWE-bench's tests are built: certain tests fail before the PR, and the PR must make them pass without breaking anything else. Spoken evidence (48:40): Terminal-Bench tasks take 'from one hour to over a week' depending on expert or junior (his reading of the human-time figure). Spoken evidence (53:25): scaffold features 'are generally optimized for the particular language model', which strengthens the point that the score belongs to the pair. misconceptions.belief: A SWE-bench score is a property of the language model.
misconceptions.why_wrong: An agent is the model plus a scaffold (L212), and the professor's summary is 'Evaluating agents = evaluating agent scaffold + language model' (L254); the same model under a different scaffold gives a different score.

misconceptions.belief: Agentic benchmarks are just harder chat benchmarks.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The shift is from what the model says to what it does (L209-L210): tasks require tool use and iteration over time (L214) and are graded by outcomes such as unit tests (L219) or a captured flag, not by judging a single response.

predict.q: A lab reports that swapping the scaffold (adding a todo list, sub-agents with clean context, and file-based memory) while keeping the model fixed raised their SWE-bench score substantially. A reviewer says 'then the benchmark is broken, since the model didn't change'. Using L212 and L254, what is the correct reading?
predict.answer: The benchmark is measuring the agent, which the lecture defines as model plus scaffold (L212); the professor says explicitly that scaffolds are very important and that evaluating agents means evaluating scaffold and model together (L253-L254). The score moved because one of the two components changed. The reviewer's concern becomes valid only if the leaderboard claims to rank models rather than agents, which is a rules-of-the-game question.
predict.why: The unit of evaluation in agentic benchmarks is the scaffold-model pair.
predict.targets_misconception: A SWE-bench score is a property of the language model.

transfer.q: A robotics group evaluates 'the same vision-language model' on a household-task benchmark with two different control loops and gets very different success rates. Transfer the lecture's agentic-evaluation lesson: what is the analogue of the scaffold, what would a leaderboard have to fix to compare models, and which SWE-bench design choice (L218-L219) is the analogue of grading by outcome?
transfer.answer: The control loop (planning, retries, memory of the scene) is the scaffold (L212); to compare models a leaderboard must fix the scaffold, or else it ranks scaffold-model pairs (L254). Grading by whether the task state is achieved is the analogue of SWE-bench's 'submit a PR, metric: unit tests' (L218-L219), an outcome check rather than a judgment of the model's output text.
transfer.why: Agent evaluation separates the decision logic around the model from the model, and grades by what the system does.
transfer.varies: domain (embodied robotics instead of software engineering) and the modality of the scaffold
transfer.invariant: the benchmark measures model plus surrounding control logic, graded on outcomes

choices: One used a harder chat-style prompt set
One leaderboard has the model wrong
Different scaffolds around the same model
check.answer: Different scaffolds around the same model
check.why: An agent is a language model plus a scaffold (L212), and the professor says evaluating agents means evaluating scaffold and model together (L254); the same model in two scaffolds is two different agents.
check.varies: a discrepancy between two published scores instead of a new domain
check.invariant: an agentic score belongs to the scaffold-model pair, not to the model alone

'One used a harder chat-style prompt set' <- misconception: 'Agentic benchmarks are just harder chat benchmarks.'

retrieval.answer: Given a codebase and an issue description, submit a PR; graded by unit tests.
