knowledge_points.label: ARC-AGI tries to isolate reasoning from knowledge
knowledge_points.statement: All the preceding benchmarks require linguistic and world knowledge, so ARC-AGI tries to measure reasoning alone with unique grid tasks that humans can fully solve but memorization cannot help with; pretrained language models did not move the needle, reasoning models did, and the goal remains hard because the benchmark is constrained to human-style reasoning and disentangling reasoning from knowledge is itself difficult.

anchors.quote: All of the tasks so far require linguistic and world knowledge ... Can we isolate reasoning from knowledge? ... Arguably, reasoning captures a more pure form of intelligence (isn't just about memorizing facts) ... ARC-AGI ... 100% solvable by humans, but challenging for AI ... Each task is unique, so memorization doesn't help
Pretrained language models didn't move the needle ... Reasoning models (o1, o3) started making things take off ... ARC-AGI-3 (March 2026): interactive environments
Goal is to disentangle reasoning from knowledge (difficult to do!) ... Constrained to human reasoning (not superhuman reasoning) ... Clearly exposes gaps in current models

anchors.ref: ARC Prize site (cited at L262; task grids, ARC-AGI-2 example and results figures shown at L267-L272)
ARC-AGI-3 technical report (cited at L276; figures shown at L277-L278)

anchors.quote: all the tasks so far require some linguistic and world knowledge. ... can we just isolate reasoning or pure fluid intelligence from a knowledge and knowing facts?
So the task was meant to be 100% solvable by humans, but challenging for AIs. ... memorizing a bunch of facts or solving previous problems shouldn't really help you that much.
pre-trained model didn't move the needle at all ... And this was exactly as the creators had intended.
this is when OpenAI released their o1 and o3 models. ... So it was really the reasoning capabilities that unlocked this.
certainly, without pre-training we wouldn't have this explosion of reasoning models. ... So arguably it was still important, but not maybe directly visible
The goal is to disentangle reasoning from knowledge. ... these still come from some prior and not sure there's anything as quote unquote pure as reasoning.
This is also constrained to human reasoning. ... So this doesn't really extend to superhuman reasoning
I think it's 64 by 64. ... you can provide this image, or you can provide it in Ascii Art

provenance.filtering_note: '100% solvable by humans' (L263) is the ARC Prize's own framing read by the professor. The results figure (images/arc-agi-results.png, L272) and ARC-AGI-3 results (L278) are shown and no score is restated; 'didn't move the needle' and 'started making things take off' (L273-L274) are the professor's reading of that chart. He does not discuss how test-time compute cost is reported on the ARC leaderboard, nor the argument that grid priors (objectness, counting) are themselves a form of knowledge, which is one reason the disentangling is 'difficult to do!' (L281). Spoken evidence (56:14-56:28): why pretraining did not help, as intended: pretrained models 'just learn what the facts are on the internet and maybe learn linguistic patterns', none of which helps directly on ARC. Spoken evidence (57:08-57:32): a caveat: 'without pre-training we wouldn't have this explosion of reasoning models', so pretraining was 'still important, but not maybe directly visible'. This does not make the misconception 'Scaling pretraining on more text is what moved ARC scores' true: he credits reasoning models with the movement (57:01). Correction (partial, 58:27-58:48): the note above says he does not make the argument that grid priors are themselves knowledge; aloud the tasks 'still come from some prior and not sure there's anything as quote unquote pure as reasoning'. Spoken evidence (58:55): superhuman reasoning means things like more olympiad gold medals or open math problems. Spoken evidence (59:36-1:00:12, Q&A): ARC-AGI-3 frames are about '64 by 64' ('I think') and can be given as an image or as ASCII art; either way the model must reason spatially. He adds that people who really cared could game ('benchmark' in the captions) probably anything (58:27).

prerequisites.note: ARC is motivated as the complement of knowledge exams (L258-L259).

misconceptions.belief: A benchmark on which humans score 100% is easy and therefore uninformative for frontier models.
misconceptions.why_wrong: ARC-AGI is '100% solvable by humans, but challenging for AI' (L263) and 'clearly exposes gaps in current models' (L283); the human ceiling is a design choice that anchors the construct, not a sign of low difficulty.

misconceptions.belief: Scaling pretraining on more text is what moved ARC scores.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor reads the results chart as pretrained language models not moving the needle and reasoning models (o1, o3) causing the jump (L273-L274); the tasks are unique so memorization from pretraining does not help (L264).

predict.q: A team proposes to improve a model's ARC-AGI score by continued pretraining on a scraped corpus of puzzle solutions and ARC-like grid examples. Which two lines of the lecture predict a small effect, and what kind of model change does the lecture associate with large ARC gains?
predict.answer: 'Each task is unique, so memorization doesn't help' (L264) and 'Pretrained language models didn't move the needle' (L273). The lecture associates large gains with reasoning models such as o1 and o3 (L274), i.e. changes in how the model computes at test time rather than what it has seen.
predict.why: The benchmark is designed so that knowledge accumulation is not the bottleneck.
predict.targets_misconception: Scaling pretraining on more text is what moved ARC scores.

transfer.q: A chemistry group wants a 'pure reasoning' benchmark for molecules and proposes novel reaction-prediction puzzles. Using the ARC section, state the two ARC design constraints they would need to copy and the one caveat the professor would raise even if they succeed.
transfer.answer: Copy: every task unique so memorization does not help (L264), and tasks that humans can fully solve so the construct is anchored to human reasoning (L263). Caveat: disentangling reasoning from knowledge is difficult (L281), and in chemistry it is worse, since reaction prediction leans on learned chemical knowledge; and such a benchmark is constrained to human reasoning, not superhuman (L282).
transfer.why: ARC's construct is defined by uniqueness and human solvability, and even then the professor flags the knowledge entanglement.
transfer.varies: domain (chemistry puzzles instead of visual grids), where knowledge is harder to exclude
transfer.invariant: a reasoning benchmark must block memorization and anchor to a human-solvable construct

check.q: A proposed 'pure reasoning' benchmark has 1,000 puzzles generated from 10 templates by changing the numbers. Which ARC-AGI design constraint does it break?
choices: Tasks need world knowledge
Humans can solve every task
Tasks are hard for humans too
Every task is unique
check.why: ARC makes each task unique so that memorization does not help (L264). Ten templates let a model learn the template and reuse it across the other 99 instances of each.
check.varies: a benchmark that fails a constraint, instead of one being designed in a new domain
check.invariant: ARC's construct rests on task uniqueness (no memorization) and full human solvability
distractor_from: 'Humans can solve every task' <- plausible: names ARC's other constraint, which templates do not break
'Tasks are hard for humans too' <- misconception: 'A benchmark on which humans score 100% is easy and therefore uninformative for frontier models.'
'Tasks need world knowledge' <- plausible: inverts ARC's goal of separating reasoning from knowledge

retrieval.q: What do all the benchmarks before ARC-AGI have in common that ARC tries to remove?
retrieval.answer: They require linguistic and world knowledge; ARC tries to isolate reasoning.

retrieval.q: Why does the professor say memorization does not help on ARC-AGI?
retrieval.answer: Each task is unique.

retrieval.q: Which class of models does the professor credit with making ARC results 'take off'?
retrieval.answer: Reasoning models (o1, o3).

retrieval.q: What is new in ARC-AGI-3?
retrieval.answer: Interactive environments.

knowledge_points.label: Safety benchmarks: harmful behaviors, policy taxonomies, jailbreaks, dual use
knowledge_points.statement: Safety evaluation operationalizes 'safe' as refusing harmful behaviors (HarmBench, from behaviors that violate laws or norms) or as compliance with risk categories drawn from regulations and company policies (AIR-Bench), and is stress-tested by jailbreaks such as GCG, which optimizes adversarial prompts on open-weight models that transfer to closed ones; what counts as safe is contextual (politics, law, norms vary by country), risks are heterogeneous, and capabilities are dual-use.

anchors.quote: What does safety mean for AI? ... HarmBench ... Based on 510 harmful behaviors that violate laws or norms
AIR-Bench ... Based on regulatory frameworks and company policies ... Taxonomized into 314 risk categories, 5694 prompts

Language models are trained to refuse harmful instructions ... Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) automatically optimizes prompts to bypass safety ... Transfers from open-weight models (Llama) to closed models (GPT-4)

Many aspects of safety are strongly contextual (politics, law, social norms - which vary across countries) ... Many risks are quite varied (hallucinations, sycophancy, abetting crimes, inequality, losing critical thinking) ... Dual-use: capable cybersecurity agents (Mythos) can be used to hack into a system or to do penetration testing

anchors.ref: HarmBench paper (cited at L290; HELM leaderboard and failure example linked at L292-L293)
AIR-Bench 2024 paper (cited at L295; overview figure shown at L298)
GCG / Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks (cited at L303; example figure shown at L305)

anchors.quote: if you think about other areas such as cars, it's pretty clear what safety means here. ... this is with decades of lobbying and figuring out what safety means for vehicles.
prompting a model with things that are meant to be harmful and expecting the model to essentially refuse. ... it turns out that's not the only thing that matters.
looking at all the regulatory frameworks in the EU, China, and the US company policies
automatic ways to optimize for prompts to bypass safety using GCG, which is basically this coordinate wise optimization algorithm. ... optimizing on open models allows us to transfer to models.
you can generate some basically gibberish and step by step plan to destroy humanity and OpenAI's model will comply.
many aspects of safety are very contextual. ... This varies across different countries.
So hallucinations is a risk ... But this is also correlated with just capabilities.
there is a dual use aspect of language models. ... which makes talking about whether these are safety risks or actually beneficial a double-edged sword.

provenance.filtering_note: '510 harmful behaviors', '314 risk categories, 5694 prompts' are read off the papers and quoted with that attribution. The crash-test photo at L287 is an analogy image. The professor does not say how HarmBench grades a refusal (it uses a classifier), how GCG's optimization works beyond 'automatically optimizes prompts', or how AIR-Bench scores compliance; the HELM failure example (L293) is linked, not described. The dual-use line (L311) names a cybersecurity agent, 'Mythos', without citation. The section ends without a summary, unlike the others. Spoken evidence (1:00:25-1:00:55): the crash-test analogy spelled out: car safety ratings rest on 'decades of lobbying and figuring out what safety means for vehicles'; AI has no such settled definition. Spoken evidence (1:01:25-1:01:38): refusing bad actors is 'probably the dominant thing' meant by safety, 'but it turns out that's not the only thing that matters'. Spoken evidence (1:01:38): AIR-Bench's regulations come from 'the EU, China, and the US' plus company policies. Correction (partial, 1:02:28-1:03:10): the note above says he does not say how GCG works beyond 'automatically optimizes prompts'; aloud it is 'basically this coordinate wise optimization algorithm', and the optimized prompt is 'basically gibberish' added to a harmful request. Spoken evidence (1:03:55-1:04:23): risks differ in how they move with capability: hallucination 'is also correlated with just capabilities' (a more accurate model hallucinates less), while abetting crimes 'might be counter to capabilities'; the captions are garbled here and nothing beyond hallucination is imported. The societal-impact view of safety 'is actually a much more complex topic than I'll have time to talk about' (1:04:30).

prerequisites.note: The dual-use example (L311) and Cybench (L231) are both about cybersecurity agents.

misconceptions.belief: Safety is a single score: the refusal rate on a harmful-prompt set.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The lecture gives two different operationalizations (behaviors that violate laws or norms at L291; regulation- and policy-derived categories at L296-L297), says safety is strongly contextual across countries (L308), and lists heterogeneous risks from hallucination to loss of critical thinking (L309); a refusal rate captures one slice.

misconceptions.belief: A closed-weight model is protected from gradient-based jailbreaks because attackers cannot compute gradients on it.
misconceptions.why_wrong: GCG optimizes the adversarial prompt on open-weight models (Llama) and the professor states that it transfers to closed models (GPT-4) (L303-L304).

predict.q: A vendor reports a near-zero attack success rate on HarmBench for its closed API and concludes it is robust to adversarial prompts optimized elsewhere. Which claim in the lecture undercuts that conclusion, and what single property of GCG does it rest on?
predict.answer: L304: GCG suffixes optimized on open-weight models like Llama transfer to closed models like GPT-4. The property is transferability of the optimized prompt across models; a benchmark of fixed behaviors does not measure robustness to prompts optimized against a surrogate.
predict.why: Static harmful-behavior sets and adaptive, transferable attacks measure different things.
predict.targets_misconception: A closed-weight model is protected from gradient-based jailbreaks because attackers cannot compute gradients on it.

transfer.q: A bank deploying an assistant in two countries with different financial-advice regulations asks for 'the safety score'. Using the lecture's AIR-Bench description and its 'what is safety?' bullets, explain why one number is the wrong deliverable and what structure a useful report would have.

So the deliverable is per-category results under each country's applicable categories, plus the heterogeneous risks that a refusal benchmark does not cover (hallucination, sycophancy, L309), rather than one aggregate.
transfer.why: The construct 'safe' changes with jurisdiction, so the metric must be indexed by category and context.
transfer.varies: domain (financial regulation) and the presence of two jurisdictions
transfer.invariant: safety is contextual and multi-category, so a single aggregate loses the construct

check.q: A vendor reports one 98% refusal rate on a harmful-prompt set and calls the model 'safe' for deployment in both Germany and Singapore. Which lecture point most directly undercuts using one number for both countries?

Closed weights block gradient attacks

check.why: The professor stresses that safety is strongly contextual, varying with politics, law and norms across countries (L308), and AIR-Bench builds categories from regulations (L296); one aggregate refusal rate cannot be correct for two jurisdictions.
check.varies: two named countries and a single refusal rate instead of a bank's financial-advice rules
check.invariant: the construct 'safe' changes with jurisdiction, so the metric must be indexed by category and context

'Closed weights block gradient attacks' <- misconception: 'A closed-weight model is protected from gradient-based jailbreaks because attackers cannot compute gradients on it.'
'Harmful behaviors are the same everywhere' <- plausible: denies the contextual point outright
check.targets_misconception: Safety is a single score: the refusal rate on a harmful-prompt set.

retrieval.answer: Harmful behaviors that violate laws or norms.

retrieval.q: What are AIR-Bench's risk categories derived from?
retrieval.answer: Regulatory frameworks and company policies.

retrieval.q: What does GCG do, and what transfer property does the professor note?
retrieval.answer: It automatically optimizes prompts to bypass safety; prompts optimized on open-weight models (Llama) transfer to closed models (GPT-4).

retrieval.q: What is the professor's dual-use example?
retrieval.answer: A capable cybersecurity agent can be used to hack into a system or to do penetration testing.

knowledge_points.label: Ecological validity: how close an evaluation is to real use
knowledge_points.statement: Ecological validity asks how well an evaluation captures real-world use: exam benchmarks are far from it, Arena prompts are real but uncontrolled, and newer efforts move closer by sourcing tasks from professionals (GDPVal across occupations weighted by GDP; MedHELM's clinician-sourced clinical tasks) or by analyzing real usage with language models (Clio), at the cost that realism and privacy pull against each other.

anchors.quote: Ecological validity: how well does an evaluation capture real-world use? ... Exam benchmarks (e.g., GPQA) are far away from real-world use ... Chatbot Arena prompts are from real people, but distribution is uncontrolled
GDPVal (OpenAI) ... 44 occupations from top 9 sectors according to US GDP ... Tasks come from professionals with ~14 years of experience
MedHELM ... Previous medical benchmarks were based on standardized exams ... 121 clinical tasks sourced from 29 clinicians, mixture of private and public datasets
Clio (Anthropic) ... Use language models to analyze real user data ... Share general patterns of what people are asking ... Unfortunately, realism and privacy are sometimes at odds with each other

anchors.ref: GDPval paper (cited at L319; figure shown at L322)
MedHELM paper (cited at L324; overview figure shown at L327; leaderboard linked at L328)
Clio paper (cited at L330; Table 4 shown at L333)

anchors.quote: So one thing that I think is an important aspect of evaluation is realism or ecological validity. ... How well does evaluation capture real-world use?
So in particular exams are very far away from real-world use. ... one could wonder whether this distribution is the right distribution of people or use cases or not.
They looked at all the top nine sectors according to US GDP, 44 different occupations ... These are professionals with about 14 years of experience.
a lot of medical benchmarks were based on standardized exams. ... for a language model, you should also not just pass medical exams and deploy them directly.
121 tasks were sourced from 29 clinicians.

who actually has the data on what people are doing? ... Well, it's the model developers. ... You can't literally go and look at people's data, but you can have language models look at the data and analyze and summarize general patterns.
sometimes realism and privacy are at odds with each other because ideally you would want actually a sample from the actual query stream.

provenance.filtering_note: '44 occupations', 'top 9 sectors', '~14 years', '121 clinical tasks', '29 clinicians' are read off the papers and quoted with that attribution; the GDPval figure and Clio Table 4 (L322, L333) are shown and their contents not restated. The professor does not say how GDPVal grades open-ended professional deliverables (the paper uses expert pairwise grading, which would connect back to the chat-benchmark section) nor how Clio preserves privacy (clustering and aggregation thresholds); both are left as pointers. 'Ecological validity' is the psychometric term and the professor uses it as given. knowledge_points.label: Train-test overlap: four routes to validity without a known training set
knowledge_points.statement: Because foundation models train on the Internet with undisclosed data, the pre-foundation discipline of fixed train-test splits is gone, and the lecture offers four routes: infer contamination from the model by exploiting exchangeability of test examples, establish reporting norms so providers disclose train-test overlap, use fresh evaluations scraped after training (though timestamps are not safe against copying), and use private evaluations such as internal code or personal writing, which is easiest for perplexity.

anchors.quote: How do we know our evaluations are valid? ... Train-test overlap ... Machine learning 101: don't train on your test set ... Pre-foundation models (ImageNet, SQuAD): well-defined train-test splits ... Today: train on the Internet and don't tell people about your data

Route 1: try to infer train-test overlap from model ... Exploit exchangeability of data points ... Route 2: encourage reporting norms (e.g., people report confidence intervals) ... Model providers should report train-test overlap

Route 3: use fresh evals ... LiveCodeBench, UncheatableEval: scrape new webpages ... Timestamps aren't always safe due to copying either ... Route 4: use private evals ... Companies use internal code bases that aren't on the Internet ... Use your personal writings ... Easiest for perplexity

anchors.ref: Proving Test Set Contamination in Black Box Language Models (cited at L347; figure shown at L348)
Language model developers should report train-test overlap (cited at L351)

anchors.quote: How do you know that when these tests are being used for training ... So the short answer is we don't know because I don't know what's in the training set.

I think train contamination is a little bit subtle. ... But questions can be derived from other sources. ... So often contamination is a much more subtle process than literally accidentally training on the test.
they also held out a private set that was not released publicly, so that they could make sure that this did not enter training.
So in a machine learning 101, you learn don't train on your test set hopefully. ... And furthermore, you don't what's in the data.
you leverage the fact that the order in which the questions in the benchmark occurs should be random. ... if the model prefers some particular order that's consistent with the benchmark
you can encourage people to report actual train-test overlap. ... in statistics you always report confidence intervals.
let's just assume that people trained on them, let's assume the worst case. ... time stamps aren't always safe either

Route 4 is to use private evaluations. ... I have a bunch of rejected papers from when I was in grad school that I never put on online ... all you need in perplexity is just you need a good data set and you can evaluate log probabilities.

provenance.filtering_note: The exchangeability test is named but not explained (L347): the cited paper compares the model's log-likelihood of the benchmark in its canonical order against shuffled orders, since an uncontaminated model has no reason to prefer the published ordering; the figure at L348 is shown and not restated. LiveCodeBench and UncheatableEval are named without links. 'Easiest for perplexity' (L360) is because a private text corpus needs no labels: one can score log-probability on one's own writing directly. The professor does not quantify how much contamination inflates any benchmark. Correction (1:09:46-1:10:26): the note above says the exchangeability test 'is named but not explained'; he explains it aloud: the order of benchmark questions 'should be random', so if the model 'prefers some particular order that's consistent with the benchmark', it was probably trained on that benchmark. Confirmation (1:12:52-1:13:09): the note's reason for 'easiest for perplexity' is what he says: 'all you need in perplexity is just you need a good data set and you can evaluate log probabilities'. Spoken evidence (26:14-27:19, Q&A in the exam section): contamination is 'a little bit subtle': labs probably do not 'literally train on the set', but 'questions can be derived from other sources. And those sources could be trained on.' His 'short answer is we don't know' (26:32) is about certainty for a given model, and he defers remedies to this section; it does not make the misconception 'Without access to the training data, contamination cannot be detected' true, since route 1 detects it from the model alone. Spoken evidence (28:12-28:32): Humanity's Last Exam keeps a private held-out set, though prompts sent to an API might still reach training ('let's hope that's the case'). Spoken evidence (1:10:41-1:11:16): route 2 by analogy with confidence intervals: a provider claiming a GPQA score 'should always provide some justification that you didn't train on the test set'. Spoken evidence (1:11:54-1:12:11): timestamps are unsafe because code posted after the cutoff may be 'derived from some other repo'. Spoken evidence (1:12:44): his own private eval, rejected grad-school papers never put online.

prerequisites.note: Exam items collected from freely available online sources (L115) are the canonical overlap risk.
Route 4's 'easiest for perplexity' (L360) presupposes the per-token log-probability measurement.

misconceptions.belief: A benchmark released after the model's training cutoff cannot be contaminated.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor says timestamps are not always safe because of copying (L355): test items are often derived from or duplicated in older web content.

misconceptions.belief: Without access to the training data, contamination cannot be detected.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Route 1 infers overlap from the model alone by exploiting exchangeability of the test examples (L346-L347), a black-box test; Route 2 asks providers to report it (L350-L351).

predict.q: A benchmark's examples are published as a JSON file in a fixed order. A black-box model assigns noticeably higher log-likelihood to the examples in that published order than to the same examples in random orders. Which route from the lecture is this, and what does the result suggest and why?
predict.answer: Route 1, inferring overlap from the model via exchangeability (L346-L347). The test examples are exchangeable, so an uncontaminated model has no reason to prefer one ordering; a preference for the published order suggests that file, in that order, was in the training data.
predict.why: Exchangeability gives a null hypothesis that can be tested without seeing the training set.
predict.targets_misconception: Without access to the training data, contamination cannot be detected.

transfer.q: A law firm wants to evaluate a vendor's model on legal drafting with no possibility of contamination and no willingness to share documents with anyone. Which route fits, what metric does the professor say is easiest under it, and what does the firm give up relative to a public benchmark?
transfer.answer: Route 4, private evals using material not on the Internet (L357-L359); the professor says this is easiest for perplexity (L360), scoring the model's log-probability on the firm's own documents without labels. The firm gives up comparability with other people's reports and the labelled, graded tasks a public benchmark provides.
transfer.why: Private data removes overlap by construction, and perplexity needs no annotation, but the result is not comparable across organizations.
transfer.varies: domain (legal drafting) and a confidentiality constraint
transfer.invariant: data the model could not have seen is uncontaminated by construction; perplexity is the label-free measurement

check.why: Route 3 (fresh evaluations scraped after training) has a stated caveat: timestamps are not safe against copying (L353-L356), since a new post can reproduce text the model already saw.
check.varies: the fresh-data route instead of the private-data route
check.invariant: each overlap route has a specific failure mode; for fresh data it is that dates do not prove novelty
distractor_from: 'It is guaranteed clean: it postdates training' <- misconception: 'A benchmark released after the model's training cutoff cannot be contaminated.'
'Overlap can't be checked without training data' <- misconception: 'Without access to the training data, contamination cannot be detected.'
'Perplexity is undefined on post-cutoff text' <- plausible: confuses novelty of text with an inability to score it
check.targets_misconception: A benchmark released after the model's training cutoff cannot be contaminated.

knowledge_points.label: Dataset quality: Verified and Platinum benchmarks, trivial agents, trace inspection
knowledge_points.statement: Benchmark validity also fails through bad items: SWE-bench was cleaned into SWE-bench Verified, Platinum versions of benchmarks remove label errors so that residual mistakes are the model's, agentic benchmarks can have insufficient test cases or let a trivial agent pass, and Docent uses an LLM to inspect agent traces to detect such problems.

anchors.quote: Dataset quality ... Fixed up SWE-Bench to produce SWE-Bench Verified ... Create Platinum versions of benchmarks
Problems with agentic benchmarks: insufficient test cases, trivial agent can solve task ... Docent: use LLM to inspect agent traces to detect problems

anchors.ref: Platinum benchmarks paper (cited at L364; two tweet images shown at L365-L366)
Best practices for rigorous agentic benchmarks (cited at L367)

anchors.quote: SWE-Bench had a bunch of problems of tasks, unit tests that weren't quite rigorous enough and other things that got fixed.
many other benchmarks that have gone through this process like GSM8K or MMLU ... something's broken around this question.
a lot of problems with the agentic benchmarks, which arguably are even harder to assess ... You might pass all the test cases but still not have a working solution.
if an agent just outputs the empty response, they can get a 38%.

Docent that uses language models to inspect agent traces to detect problems. ... you always look at the output and try to audit it to make sure that you actually think you're measuring what you think you're measuring.

provenance.filtering_note: This is the sparsest part of the lecture: four one-line pointers. The professor does not say what was wrong with SWE-bench items (the Verified post describes underspecified issues and over-strict tests, screened by human annotators) nor what 'Platinum' means operationally (the paper revises or removes mislabeled items so top models' errors are real errors); the two tweet images at L365-L366 are shown and not restated. 'Insufficient test cases' means a wrong patch passes; 'trivial agent can solve task' means the task leaks its answer or the grader is too lenient. Docent's method is only named. Correction (partial, 1:13:16-1:13:36): the note above says the professor does not say what was wrong with SWE-bench items; aloud: 'unit tests that weren't quite rigorous enough and other things'. Spoken evidence (1:14:04-1:14:16): two Platinum examples from the tweet images are read aloud (a question about a curve that is not given, and 'Does the baby have socks on? No, there's no way to tell'). Spoken evidence (1:14:16-1:14:34): agentic benchmarks are 'even harder to assess' because an item is a whole environment, not a question with answers. Spoken evidence (1:14:50): 'if an agent just outputs the empty response, they can get a 38%'; the captions say 'TorchBench', but the cited paper (arXiv 2507.02825) reports this for τ-bench: a trivial agent returning empty responses passes 38% of airline tasks because intentionally impossible tasks accept an empty reply (checked against the paper; a caption error, not a slip). Spoken evidence (1:15:17-1:15:41): Docent is 'a qualitative response to our very quantitative heavy way of benchmarking', and the advice: whenever you build or run a benchmark, 'always look at the output'.

prerequisites.note: SWE-bench and agentic benchmarks were introduced at L216-L254; their quality problems are deferred here.
Second subsection of validity() (L362), after train-test overlap.

misconceptions.belief: If a benchmark is graded by executable tests, its items are correct by construction.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor lists 'insufficient test cases' and 'trivial agent can solve task' as problems specific to agentic benchmarks (L367): tests can pass wrong patches, and a task can be solvable without the intended capability. SWE-bench itself needed a Verified cleanup (L363).

misconceptions.belief: When top models plateau below 100% on a benchmark, the remaining gap is model capability.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Platinum versions exist because some of that gap is label error in the benchmark (L364); only after removing bad items can residual errors be attributed to the model.

predict.q: An agentic coding benchmark reports that an 'agent' that simply replies 'done' without editing any file scores 12%. Which problem from L367 does this reveal, and what would the Verified-style fix (L363) and the Docent-style check (L368) each do about it?
predict.answer: 'Trivial agent can solve task' (L367): some tasks pass their tests with no work, so their tests are insufficient. A Verified-style fix has humans screen and remove or repair those items (L363); a Docent-style check runs an LLM over the agent traces to flag tasks where success occurred without the expected actions (L368).
predict.why: Outcome-graded benchmarks are only as good as their graders; both fixes audit the items, one by hand and one with a model.
predict.targets_misconception: If a benchmark is graded by executable tests, its items are correct by construction.

transfer.q: A radiology benchmark finds the three best models all miss the same 4% of cases. Before concluding the models share a blind spot, which step from this section applies, what would it do, and how would the conclusion change if those cases turn out to be mislabeled?
transfer.answer: Create a Platinum version (L364): audit and relabel or remove items that are wrong or ambiguous. If the shared 4% are label errors, the 'blind spot' is the benchmark's, not the models', and the models are closer to the ceiling than the raw score showed.
transfer.why: Convergent errors across strong models are a signal to inspect the labels, which is the motivation for Platinum benchmarks.
transfer.varies: domain (medical imaging) and the evidence (convergent errors) prompting the audit
transfer.invariant: residual error is attributable to the model only after item quality is verified

check.q: The top models plateau at 91% on a math benchmark. An audit finds that on 6% of the items the answer key is wrong and the models' answers are actually correct, and a Platinum-style version fixes those keys. Do the top models' scores go up, down, or stay the same?
check.answer: up: answers that were marked wrong against bad keys now count as correct
check.why: Platinum versions remove label errors so that residual mistakes are the model's (L364); part of the plateau gap was the benchmark's, so scores rise toward the real ceiling.
check.varies: a math benchmark with an explicit audit result, asked as a direction
check.invariant: a benchmark score mixes model errors with item errors; cleaning items removes the latter
check.targets_misconception: When top models plateau below 100% on a benchmark, the remaining gap is model capability.

retrieval.answer: SWE-bench Verified.

retrieval.answer: Insufficient test cases, and a trivial agent being able to solve the task.

knowledge_points.label: No one true evaluation: purposes, methods vs models, rules of the game
knowledge_points.statement: There is no one true evaluation; the right one depends on whether the question is a purchase decision, a measurement of raw capability, an accounting of benefits and harms, or developer feedback; pre-foundation ML evaluated methods on standardized splits while today we mostly evaluate models or systems where anything goes (the nanogpt speedrun, fixed data and time to a validation loss, is a surviving methods evaluation), and either way one must state the rules of the game along the axes of difficulty, realism and validity.

anchors.quote: There is no one true evaluation; it depends on what question you're trying to answer ... make a purchase decision ... measure the raw capabilities of a model ... understand the benefits + harms of a model ... Model developers want to get feedback to improve the model

Pre-foundation models, we evaluated methods (standardized train-test splits) ... Today, we're (mostly) evaluating models/systems (anything goes) ... nanogpt speedrun: fixed data, compute time to get to a particular validation loss
Evaluating methods encourage algorithmic innovation from researchers ... Evaluating models/systems is useful for downstream users ... Either way, we need to define the rules of the game!

There is no one true evaluation; choose the evaluation depending on what you're trying to measure ... Clearly state the rules of the game (methods versus models versus agents) ... Considerations: difficulty, realism, validity

anchors.ref: Karpathy nanogpt speedrun post (cited at L385; screenshot shown)

anchors.quote: there's no one evaluation to rule them all. ... you have to be very clear about what the purpose is. ... And I think often this is not really stated clearly.
before foundation models, researchers evaluated methods because we have these trained test splits. ... And today, we're mostly evaluating models and systems where anything goes.
So the NanoGPT speedrun is deliberately a way to evaluate an algorithm ... which is useful because that is the thing that is actually going to get shipped
It's hard to have really real and difficult and ecologically valid. ... you will have to choose which one you're willing to compromise on.

provenance.filtering_note: The speedrun screenshot (images/karpathy-nanogpt-speedrun.png, L385) shows record times that are not restated. The professor's three considerations in the takeaway (difficulty, realism, validity, L30) are the names of the exam/Arena, realism() and validity() sections respectively; 'methods versus models versus agents' (L29) adds agents to the L380-L381 dichotomy, pointing back to the scaffold-plus-model point at L254. He does not discuss cost or test-time compute as a rule of the game, though Artificial Analysis cost (L48-L49) and ARC's compute budgets implicitly raise it. Spoken evidence (1:16:01): purposes are 'often ... not really stated clearly'. Spoken evidence (1:16:47-1:16:57): why the old regime evaluated methods: with fixed train-test splits 'the only thing that was varying is the actual algorithm'. Spoken evidence (1:17:14): evaluating end models is useful because 'that is the thing that is actually going to get shipped'. Spoken evidence (1:17:55-1:18:19): the takeaway's three considerations trade off: 'It's hard to have really real and difficult and ecologically valid' and uncontaminated, so one compromises according to the goal; L30 only lists them.

prerequisites.note: The closing 'no one true evaluation' (L373) answers the opening 'how good is it?' (L12, L42).
'methods versus models versus agents' (L29) relies on the scaffold-plus-model distinction (L254).
how_to_think_about_evaluation() follows validity() in main() (L24-L25).

misconceptions.belief: Evaluating a model on a benchmark is the same kind of claim as the pre-foundation practice of evaluating a method on a benchmark.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Methods evaluation fixed the training data and split so that differences were attributable to the algorithm (L380); models evaluation lets anything go in training (L381), so a score reflects data, compute and scaffold as well as method. The nanogpt speedrun is cited as a rare surviving methods evaluation (L384).

misconceptions.belief: The goal of evaluation research is to converge on the single best benchmark.
misconceptions.why_wrong: 'There is no one true evaluation' (L28, L373); the four purposes at L374-L377 call for different evaluations, and the lecture's actionable advice is to state the rules of the game (L390), not to pick a winner.

predict.q: A paper claims 'our new optimizer is better' and supports it by training a model with it on a proprietary 10T-token corpus and beating a public model on MMLU. A second paper claims the same optimizer is better by lowering the time to reach a fixed validation loss on the fixed nanogpt speedrun data. Which paper is doing a methods evaluation in the lecture's sense, and what is confounded in the other?
predict.answer: The second: fixed data and a fixed target loss (L384) make the optimizer the only variable, which is evaluating a method (L380). The first evaluates a model/system (L381): the proprietary data, compute and any other training differences are confounded with the optimizer, so the MMLU gain cannot be attributed to it.
predict.why: Methods evaluation requires standardized inputs so that the method is the thing varied.
predict.targets_misconception: Evaluating a model on a benchmark is the same kind of claim as the pre-foundation practice of evaluating a method on a benchmark.

transfer.q: A government agency, a model vendor's training team, and a small business each ask you 'which evaluation should we run?'. Match each to one of the four purposes at L374-L377, name a benchmark family from the lecture that fits each, and state the single piece of advice the professor says applies to all of them.
transfer.answer: Agency: understand benefits and harms (L376), safety benchmarks like HarmBench or AIR-Bench. Training team: developer feedback to improve the model (L377), perplexity and exam benchmarks that give smooth, cheap signal. Small business: a purchase decision for a use case (L374), a realistic task set close to their work (GDPVal-style, or their own private eval). To all: define the rules of the game (L390), stating what is being evaluated (method, model or agent) and the difficulty, realism and validity choices (L29-L30).
transfer.why: The purpose selects the evaluation; the rules of the game make the result interpretable regardless.
transfer.varies: the asker's purpose (three different purposes from the lecture's list), Barnett-Ceci functional context
transfer.invariant: evaluation choice follows from the question asked, and the rules must be stated explicitly

check.q: A vendor's training team wants a cheap, smooth signal to compare checkpoints every few hours. Which purpose from L374-L377 is this, with a fitting evaluation?

check.why: Feedback to improve the model (L377) calls for frequent, smooth, cheap signal such as perplexity; purchase decisions and harm accounting are other purposes, and there is no single best benchmark to converge on.

'Purchase decision: a private task set' <- plausible: picks a realistic evaluation that answers a buyer's question, not a trainer's
'Benefits and harms: HarmBench refusals' <- plausible: picks the agency's purpose
check.targets_misconception: The goal of evaluation research is to converge on the single best benchmark.

retrieval.answer: Difficulty, realism, validity.
